author: Anonymous
genre: disputation / martyr act in dialogue form
occasion: Martianus, consular prefect under Decius, has Achatius brought before him to require sacrifice with him to the emperor's gods. The narrator presents the interrogation as remembrance of the glorious deeds of God's servants, ending with imprisonment and referral of the record to Decius; the clause describing why Achatius was singled out is corrupt and uncertain.
argument: Achatius argues that Christians most honor the emperor by constant prayer for his life, just rule, armies, and world peace, but sacrifice is owed to the true God, not to a man. He identifies that God as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the Most High Adonai above cherubim and seraphim, and rejects visible gods: Apollo as lustful, ignorant, servile and deadly in the girl's flight, the Hyacinth discus killing, and service with Neptune, Asclepius as lightning-struck, adulterous Venus and the rest of that sort in an unreadable lacuna, and then separately refuses Martianus's invitation to feast to Jupiter and Juno by asking how to sacrifice to one whose tomb is in Crete. Threatened with sacrifice or death, he compares Martianus to Dalmatian robbers, appeals to public law that punishes fornication, adultery, theft, corruption, sorcery and murder, cites judgment sayings, and says condemnation for worshiping the true God is the judge's will not law, and he must obey God rather than deny Christ who will judge living and dead. He confesses God's Son as the Word of truth and grace, Jesus Christ, denying begetting by human intercourse, contrasting Adam first formed by God's hand and given soul and spirit with the Son proceeding as Word from God's heart, debating body and mind, and then answering the separate demand to gather those of the catholic law that they are ruled by God's precept not his nod, refusing names written in the heavenly book and rejecting the magic charge.

outline.move: The narrator introduces Martianus and the bringing in of Achatius in a corrupt clause, and Achatius says Christians pray continually for emperor, soldiers and world but will not sacrifice to a man.
Martianus asks which god Achatius prays to, and Achatius names the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the Most High Adonai over cherubim and seraphim and explains seraphim.

Achatius rejects Apollo, lightning-struck Asclepius, adulterous Venus and the rest of that sort in an unreadable lacuna with Apollo's flight, Hyacinth, and service with Neptune, and then when Martianus invites him to feast to Jupiter and Juno he asks how to sacrifice to one whose tomb is in Crete.
Under the order sacrifice or die, Achatius compares Martianus to Dalmatian robbers, appeals to public law, quotes judgment sayings, and says he must not deny God who will judge living and dead.

After confessing Jesus Christ as Word of truth from God's heart, denying bodily generation and disputing body and mind, Achatius in a following exchange answers Martianus's appeal to Cataphryges converts and order to gather all of the catholic law by saying they are ruled by God's precept not his nod.
Achatius refuses to give names written in the heavenly book and rejects the charge of being magi, saying Christians destroy man-made gods and fear the Maker, Father and deliverer.

Pressed for names in the ambiguous vocor clause, the speaker gives Achatius, Agathangelus, Piso and Menander forms, is jailed for Decius, and Decius laughs at the record, gives Martianus Pamphylia, and returns Achatius to his own standing and law on the fourth kalends of April.

scripture: Quotations are Latin without book names, introduced by prophet cries, it is written, and again. Psalm wording follows old Latin / LXX numbering, about one number lower than modern Hebrew numbering: Eructavit cor meum verbum bonum is Ps 44 Vg = Ps 45:1 modern. Non est qui inquirat deum etc. is Ps 13 Vg = Ps 14 modern, also Rom 3:11-12. Ut iudicas etc. reflects Matt 7:1-2. Qui me denegaverit reflects Matt 10:33. Adam formed from mud reflects Gen 2:7. Cite in modern form as Gen, Ps, Matt, Rom with chapter:verse, noting Vg/LXX psalm number where relevant.
uncertain: Composition date and original language: dramatic date is under Decius, but whether the Latin preserves a contemporary record or is a later hagiographic disputation is not shown.
Opening motive: quem [secutum] quoddam ac refugium illius religionis audierat is bracketed as corrupt, with R reading Antiochiae regionis for illius religionis; leader and refuge is not certain.

Speaker's names: whether Achatius/Agathangelus is Acacius of Antioch, and whether Piso Troianorum episcopus and Menander presbyter are separate persons or further predicates of vocor in the same clause.
Places and persons: whether Piso Troianorum means Troy/Ilion or Troas, and who Menander was.
Cataphryges: source calls them homines religionis antiquae converted to imperial rites; identification as Montanists or any historical event is conjecture.
Corrupt readings marked in brackets: secutum, Antiochiae regionis for illius religionis, et/scan, porientis unreadable; et ceteris after Venus belongs to that unreadable sort.
Judgment sayings: exact sources and numbering for Omnis in quo iudicat, sic et iudicabitur and Ut iudicas, sic et iudicaberis, et ut facis, sic et erit tibi.
Ending: aestimationi propriae et legi suae reddidit and the Pamphylia appointment suggest release rather than martyrdom, but the legal outcome is unclear.
Dalmatae comparison and quarto kalendas Aprilis: whether these preserve local historical detail or rhetorical dating.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Apollo as lustful, ignorant, servile and deadly in the girl's flight, the Hyacinth discus killing, and service with Neptune
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: qui infelix cum puellae amore flagraret currebat attonitus, ignarus perditurum se optatissimam praedam...disco illum quem optabat videre occidit. qui cum Neptuno aliquando servivit, ipsi qui aliena pecora servavit
_unresolved_facts.fix: Apollo's flight with the girl: he was 'ignarus perditurum se optatissimam praedam' (unaware he would destroy the prey he most desired), not 'deadly in the girl's flight'—he failed to catch her, not killed her. The discus killing of Hyacinth is correct. The service with Neptune is described as 'qui aliena pecora servavit' (who guarded others' cattle/ flocks), i.e., Apollo served as a herdsman for Neptune.

_unresolved_facts.claim: separately refuses Martianus's invitation to feast to Jupiter and Juno
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: propterea te venire mecum ad Iovem Iunonemque praecipio, ut simul celebrantes dulce convivium numinibus quae sunt digna reddamus. respondit Achatius: Quomodo hic sacrificabo illi cuius sepulcrum esse constat in Creta? numquid resurrexit a mortuis?
_unresolved_facts.fix: Achatius does not 'separately refuse'—he responds directly to the invitation to feast to Jupiter and Juno by asking how he can sacrifice to one whose tomb is in Crete. The 'separately' implies a distinct exchange; it is part of the same continuous exchange about Apollo and other gods.

_unresolved_facts.claim: condemnation for worshiping the true God is the judge's will not law
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: non legis, sed iudicis voluntate condemnor
_unresolved_facts.fix: Achatius says 'non legis, sed iudicis voluntate condemnor' (not by law, but by the judge's will I am condemned)—this refers to his own condemnation, not 'condemnation for worshiping the true God' as a general claim. The brief makes it sound like a principled statement about the nature of such condemnation; it's a personal accusation against Martianus.

_unresolved_facts.claim: answering the separate demand to gather those of the catholic law
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: omnes catholicae legis collige Christianos et cum his religionem nostri imperatoris attende. veniat tecum omnis populus, ex tuo pendet arbitrio: respondit Achatius: Illi omnes non meo nutu, sed dei praecepto reguntur
_unresolved_facts.fix: Martianus demands 'collige' (gather/collect) all Christians of the catholic law and 'attende' (pay attention to/give heed to) the religion of their emperor with them; he does not demand that Achatius 'gather those of the catholic law' as if collecting them for a meeting, but rather that Achatius bring them to follow imperial religion. Achatius responds they are ruled by God's precept, not his nod.

_unresolved_facts.claim: separately refuses Martianus's invitation to feast to Jupiter and Juno
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: propterea te venire mecum ad Iovem Iunonemque praecipio, ut simul celebrantes dulce convivium numinibus quae sunt digna reddamus. respondit Achatius: Quomodo hic sacrificabo illi cuius sepulcrum esse constat in Creta?
_unresolved_facts.fix: This is not a 'separate' refusal but the direct response in the same exchange; remove 'separately'.

_unresolved_facts.claim: the speaker gives Achatius, Agathangelus, Piso and Menander forms
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Achatius dicor, et si proprium nomen meum exploras, vocor Agathangelus, et Piso Troianorum episcopus, et Menander presbyter
_unresolved_facts.fix: The syntax is ambiguous: 'vocor Agathangelus, et Piso Troianorum episcopus, et Menander presbyter' could mean 'I am called Agathangelus, and [I am] Piso bishop of the Trojans, and [I am] Menander the presbyter' OR 'I am called Agathangelus, and [there is] Piso bishop of the Trojans, and [there is] Menander the presbyter.' The brief assumes the first but presents it as fact; should note uncertainty.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Decius laughs at the record, gives Martianus Pamphylia, and returns Achatius to his own standing and law
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: versum in risum est et Martiano praefecturam Pamphyliae mox dedit, Achatium vero vehementer admirans aestimationi propriae et legi suae reddidit
_unresolved_facts.fix: Decius 'versum in risum est' (was turned to laughter / burst out laughing) at the 'alterationem iam redditae responsionis' (the strange/wondrous exchange of the given reply), not simply 'laughs at the record.' 'Aestimationi propriae et legi suae reddidit' means he returned Achatius to his own estimation/assessment and his own law, i.e., left him to his own devices under his own legal status—not clearly 'returns Achatius to his own standing and law' as if a positive legal outcome.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Piso...may be a further title of the speaker or a separate bishop; syntax uncertain
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: vocor Agathangelus, et Piso Troianorum episcopus, et Menander presbyter
_unresolved_facts.fix: The brief says 'may be a further title of the speaker or a separate bishop; syntax uncertain' but the 'who' field should reflect that if Piso is a separate person, he is a bishop of the Trojans/Troas; if the same person, the speaker claims that title. The current 'who' is vague about what Piso would be.

_unresolved_facts.claim: et iterum continues the same quoted voice, not a new speaker
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: scriptum est enim: Omnis in quo iudicat, sic et iudicabitur. et iterum: Ut iudicas, sic et iudicaberis, et ut facis, sic et erit tibi
_unresolved_facts.fix: The brief's parenthetical claim that 'et iterum continues the same quoted voice, not a new speaker' is an interpretation, not a source marking. The source simply has 'et iterum:' introducing a second saying. This interpretive note doesn't belong in 'how_marked' which should describe source markings.

The source form is 'Aesculapio' (dative/ablative of Aesculapius). The brief maps 'Aesculapius' to 'Asclepius' but the source form listed in names should be 'Aesculapius' or 'Aesculapio', not 'Aesculapius' as if that's the brief's form. Actually the names field has 'Aesculapius' as key and 'Asclepius' as value, but the source has 'Aesculapio'. The key should match the source form more closely, or note the Latin form.
